subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Carnot Limit
description: A quick, practical guide to The Carnot Limit.

hook.text: In 1824, a French physicist proved that no heat engine can ever be perfectly efficient.

buildup.text: Sadi Carnot showed that converting heat to work always leaves some energy behind as waste.

discovery.text: Maximum efficiency depends only on the temperature gap between the hot and cold sides.

twist.text: Even a theoretically perfect gasoline engine could never exceed about 60 percent efficiency.

climax.text: Real engines reach about half the Carnot limit due to friction, heat loss, and incomplete burning.

punchline.text: Physics itself caps how good an engine can ever get.

quiz.question: What does the Carnot limit describe?
options: Maximum theoretical efficiency of a heat engine

details.summary: The Carnot limit is a thermodynamic law that caps the maximum theoretical efficiency of any heat engine based on the temperature difference between its hot combustion and cool exhaust, limiting even perfect engines to roughly 60 percent efficiency.
details.whyItMatters: The Carnot limit explains why combustion engines waste so much energy as heat. No amount of engineering can overcome this physical law, which is why electric motors with no combustion are fundamentally more efficient.
takeaways: No heat engine can convert 100 percent of heat into work
Maximum efficiency depends on the temperature ratio of source and sink
Real engines achieve 25 to 50 percent of the Carnot limit at best

faq.question: What efficiency do modern car engines actually achieve?
faq.answer: Typical gasoline engines achieve 25 to 35 percent thermal efficiency. F1 engines push above 50 percent. Diesel engines reach 40 to 45 percent. The remaining energy is lost as waste heat through the exhaust and cooling system.

faq.question: Why are electric motors not limited by the Carnot equation?
faq.answer: Electric motors convert electricity directly to motion without combustion. They are not heat engines and therefore not subject to the Carnot limit. This is why electric motors achieve 90 to 95 percent efficiency.
